payload.wikitext: {{Short description|Genus of ornithopod dinosaur}} {{under construction}} {{Speciesbox | fossil_range = [[Early Cretaceous]], {{fossilrange|Barremian|Barremian|[[Barremian]]}} | image = Paludohadros proudlovii.png | image_caption = [[Life restoration]] | display_parents = 2 | genus = Paludohadros | parent_authority = Sacamoto et al., [[2026 in archosaur paleontology|2026]] | species = proudlovii | authority = Sacamoto et al., 2026 }} '''''Paludohadros''''' ({{lit|swamp hadrosauroid}}) is an [[extinct]] genus of [[hadrosauroid]] ornithopod dinosaur known from the [[Early Cretaceous]] ([[Barremian]] age) [[Weald Clay Formation]] and likely also the [[Wessex Formation]] of the United Kingdom. The genus contains a [[Monotypic taxon|single species]], '''''Paludohadros proudlovii''''', known from a partial skull and skeleton, as well as various isolated remains. It is one of several [[iguanodontia]]n dinosaurs known from the [[Weald Basin]], though all others are from older [[Valanginian]] rock layers, including ''[[Barilium]]'', ''[[Hypselospinus]]'', and ''[[Kukufeldia]]''. == Discovery and naming == On July 22, 2001, the British [[Geologists' Association]] conducted a field trip to [[Smokejack Clay Pit]] (now Ewhurst Works) near the village of [[Ewhurst, Surrey|Ewhurst]] in [[Surrey]], UK. This site, which exposes outcrops of the [[Weald Clay Formation]], is known for yielding the holotype specimen of the [[spinosaurid]] theropod ''[[Baryonyx walkeri]]'' in 1983. During the 2001 excursion, Geoff Toye discovered a partial iguanodontian skull and skeleton in the same rock layer that produced the ''Baryonyx'' specimen, albeit around {{convert|100|m|ft}} west. The site was excavated throughout the next two weeks with the assistance of the [[Natural History Museum, London|Natural History Museum]] (NHMUK), during which several limb bones were recovered, but only three vertebrae, all of which came from the tail. Two ''Baryonyx'' teeth were recovered as well, a possible indication that the iguanodont carcass was [[scavenged]]. An initial report by the Geologists' Association in October, 2001 identified the remains as belonging to a juvenile ''[[Iguanodon]]''. In 2008, a formal publication described the palaeoenvironment of the quarry that yielded this specimen, focused on fossil [[pollen]] and [[ostracod]]s. The iguanodont fossil was ultimately donated to the NHMUK, where it is now permanently [[Accession number (cultural property)|accessioned]] as specimen NHMUK PV R 16396. It consists of a partial skull (including several bones of the cranium, braincase, palate, and mandible) and various [[postcrania]]l remains, including {{dinogloss|rib}} fragments, the right {{dinogloss|pectoral girdle}}, much of both forelimbs, the right {{dinogloss|ischium}} (a {{dinogloss|pelvis|pelvic bone}}), parts of both hindlimbs, and three {{dinogloss|caudals|caudal (tail) vertebrae}}. In a 2021 review of Smokejacks fossils, these "''Iguanodon''" remains were instead regarded as belonging to the related genus ''[[Mantellisaurus]]''. In 2026, Ricardo J. Sacamoto and colleagues [[Species description|described]] ''Paludohadros proudlovii'' as a new genus and species of hadrosauroid dinosaur based on these fossil remains, designating NHMUK PV R 16396 as the [[holotype]] specimen. Four {{dinogloss|humeri}} and four {{dinogloss|tibiae}} from Smokejack Pit, described by W. H. E. Rivett in 1953 and 1956, were referred to this species. The [[Genus|generic name]], ''Paludohadros'', combines the [[Latin]] word {{lang|la|[[:wikt:palus#Latin|palūs]]}}, meaning {{gloss|swamp}}, with the [[Greek language|Greek]] {{lang|grc|[[:wikt:ἁδρός|ἁδρός]]}} ({{lang|grc|hadrós}}), a suffix often used in hadrosauroid genus names meaning {{gloss|stout}} or {{gloss|robust}}. This references the swampy environment this taxon would have inhabited during the Cretaceous, as well as the current muddy conditions of the type locality. The [[Specific name (zoology)|specific name]], ''proudlovii'', honors William Proudlove, who managed the Smokejack Pit and died in 2000, shortly before the excavation of the holotype. The studies authors also suggested a [[surangular]] bone (NHMUK PV R 105a) from an unknown locality of the [[Wessex Formation]] of the Isle of Wight was likely attributable to ''Paludohadros''. == Description == ''Paludohadros'' is estimated to have been about {{Convert|5|m}} long.{{Cite web |last=Lazaro |first=Enrico de |date=2026-10-27 |title=New Species of Iguanodontian Dinosaur Discovered in England {{!}} Sci.News |url=https://www.sci.news/paleontology/paludohadros-proudlovii-15156.html |access-date=2026-11-01 |website=Sci.News: Breaking Science News |language=en-US}} The skeleton of ''Paludohadros'' is distinguished from other iguanodontians by several anatomical characters, including the number of ridges on the teeth of the lower jaw, a well developed upward (dorsally) projecting lateral process (extension) of the [[surangular]] bone of the lower jaw, the distal condyle of the humerus having ridge that projects proximally (towards the body), the ischium curves backwards and downwards (posteroventrally) and has a well developed boot, and a tibia with bosses (growths) on the (proximal) end closest to the knee joint. == Phylogeny == A phylogeny conducted by
